opening.text: Have you ever stood at the edge of a decision and could not see what was on the other side? A new job. A move to a new place. A promise you were asked to make. You could not see how it would end. You had to choose without knowing.
Most of the important choices in life are like that. We do not get all the answers first. We get enough light for the next step.
That is where faith lives. Today I want to talk about faith in Jesus Christ: what it is, where it comes from, how it works, and how we keep it strong.

mainMessage.text: Faith in Jesus Christ is a gift from God. It begins with a desire to believe, it grows as we hear God’s word, and it becomes strong as we act on it.

blocks.text: What is the first principle of the gospel? We often just say, faith. But the more exact answer is faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Faith always has a person at its center. We do not simply believe in believing. We believe in Him.
Paul wrote to Saints who were being tested. They needed to be reminded of what faith really is.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Notice that faith has substance and evidence. It is not a guess in the dark. It rests on something. For the Saints, it rested on the promises of God and on the life of His Son.
Alma was teaching a humble group of Zoramites who had been cast out of their places of worship. They wanted to believe, but they did not know where to start. Alma gave them a simple truth.
And now as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true.
So faith is not having every answer. It is trusting what is true even when we cannot yet see all of it. We hope for things that are not seen, but that are true.

President Russell M. Nelson taught what happens when we place that trust in the Savior. In his talk “Christ Is Risen; Faith in Him Will Move Mountains,” from the April 2021 general conference, he said:
Jesus Christ will increase your ability to move the mountains in your life.

Every one of us has a mountain. It may be grief, fear, a habit we cannot break, or a worry about someone we love. Faith in Jesus Christ does not always remove the mountain on the day we ask. But it changes what we are able to do with it.
President James E. Faust added that faith and hope go together. In his talk “Hope, an Anchor of the Soul,” from the October 1999 general conference, he said:
Hope is trust in God’s promises, faith that if we act now, the desired blessings will be fulfilled in the future.
Trust, and then act. Keep those two words in mind. We will come back to them.
If faith is a gift, where do we receive it? Paul answered this when he wrote to the Saints in Rome.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

Faith comes by hearing the word of God. That puts something in our hands. We cannot control every circumstance, but we can control what we listen to. If we want more faith, we put ourselves in the way of God’s word.
Mormon, as he told the history of the Nephites, stopped to share what he had learned about the power of the word of God.

Yea, we see that whosoever will may lay hold upon the word of God, which is quick and powerful, which shall divide asunder all the cunning and the snares and the wiles of the devil, and lead the man of Christ in a strait and narrow course across that everlasting gulf of misery which is prepared to engulf the wicked—
The word “whosoever” matters. It means this is for any of us. And the word “will” matters too. It is a choice.

Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained how this works. In his talk “Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

When we want to speak to God, we pray. And when we want Him to speak to us, we search the scriptures; for His words are spoken through His prophets. He will then teach us as we listen to the promptings of the Holy Spirit.

Think of it as a conversation. In prayer, we speak. In the scriptures, we listen. A person who prays but never reads is only doing half of the conversation. We also listen when we hear the prophets and apostles speak at general conference. Each time, our faith gets another piece of what it needs.
Here is where trust and action meet. James wrote to Saints who said they believed but whose lives had not changed.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.

Faith that never acts is like a seed kept in a drawer. It is alive in the package, but it will never become anything. James is not asking us to earn God’s love. He is showing us what real faith looks like when it is alive.
John the Baptist faced the same thing. Many who came to be baptized said that they were safe because they were descendants of Abraham.

Then said he to the multitude that came forth to be baptized of him, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, That God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
A family name or a church record does not carry us. Fruits do. Fruits are the visible result of what we believe.

What do the fruits of faith look like? A parent who keeps teaching when the child does not listen. A neighbor who visits the lonely one. A person who forgives. A person who keeps a covenant when it costs something. Faith becomes clear in these ordinary acts.

When we act on faith, God works in our lives. Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained how faith is made stronger. In his talk “The Sustaining Power of Faith in Times of Uncertainty and Testing,” from the April 2003 general conference, he said:

You can learn to use faith more effectively by applying this principle taught by Moroni: ‘. . . ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith’ \[Ether 12:6; italics added\]. Thus, every time you try your faith, that is, act in worthiness on an impression, you will receive the confirming evidence of the Spirit. Those feelings will fortify your faith. As you repeat that pattern, your faith will become stronger.
So our faith grows in a pattern. We feel a prompting. We act. The Spirit confirms. And we are ready for the next step.
Moroni wrote about this near the end of the Book of Mormon, as he explained why people should not demand proof before they act.

And now, I, Moroni, would speak somewhat concerning these things; I would show unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.
Many people say they will believe when they see a sign. The Lord teaches that the order is the other way around. He taught this to the Saints through the Prophet Joseph Smith.

But, behold, faith cometh not by signs, but signs follow those that believe.
Yea, signs come by faith, not by the will of men, nor as they please, but by the will of God.

We do not demand that God prove Himself first. We choose to trust Him, and then we see His hand. And a sign alone does not make faith. Nephi’s older brothers, Laman and Lemuel, were visited by an angel.
And it came to pass as they smote us with a rod, behold, an angel of the Lord came and stood before them, and he spake unto them, saying: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod?
An angel stood before them, and almost at once they were complaining again. Seeing is not the same as believing. Faith is a choice of the heart.
Some of us carry something heavy today. Faith does not always lift it. But it does change how we carry it.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke honestly about this. In his talk “Healing the Sick,” from the April 2010 general conference, he said:

As we exercise the undoubted power of the priesthood of God and as we treasure His promise that He will hear and answer the prayer of faith, we must always remember that faith and the healing power of the priesthood cannot produce a result contrary to the will of Him whose priesthood it is.
God hears the prayer of faith, and His will is wiser than ours. When the answer is different from what we asked, we can still lean on Him.
Paul wrote to Hebrew Saints who were suffering for what they believed. He reminded them of a promise.

Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.
“I will never leave thee.” That is the promise that holds us on a hard day. Paul also pointed the Saints to those who had gone before them in faith, such as Abraham and Moses.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
They did not see every promise come true. They saw them from far off, and they held on. And God kept faith with them.
Helaman wrote to Captain Moroni about his own people. They were few, weak, and in danger. They did the one thing they could do.

Therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.
Yea, and it came to pass that the Lord our God did visit us with assurances that he would deliver us; yea, insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him.
They prayed, and God gave them peace and added to their faith. That is how it works. We bring what little we have, and God makes it more.
Faith can grow weak if we leave it alone. How do we keep it alive? Alma gave the Zoramites a picture they could understand.

But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.
Now, we will compare the word unto a seed. Now, if ye give place, that a seed may be planted in your heart, behold, if it be a true seed, or a good seed, if ye do not cast it out by your unbelief, that ye will resist the Spirit of the Lord, behold, it will begin to swell within your breasts; and when you feel these swelling motions, ye will begin to say within yourselves—It must needs be that this is a good seed, or that the word is good, for it beginneth to enlarge my soul; yea, it beginneth to enlighten my understanding, yea, it beginneth to be delicious to me.
The starting point is small: a desire to believe. Alma did not ask for a great deal. He asked them to give the word a place in their hearts and see what happens.
But a seed needs care. Alma went on to tell them what happens when we care for it, and what happens when we do not.

But if ye neglect the tree, and take no thought for its nourishment, behold it will not get any root; and when the heat of the sun cometh and scorcheth it, because it hath no root it withers away, and ye pluck it up and cast it out.
But if ye will nourish the word, yea, nourish the tree as it beginneth to grow, by your faith with great diligence, and with patience, looking forward to the fruit thereof, it shall take root; and behold it shall be a tree springing up unto everlasting life.
The tree does not die because the seed was bad. It dies from neglect. Nephi told his people how to avoid that.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained what it means to feast. In his talk “Living by Scriptural Guidance,” from the October 2000 general conference, he said:

To feast means to savor. We savor the scriptures by studying them in a spirit of delightful discovery and faithful obedience. When we feast upon the words of Christ, they . . . become an integral part of our nature.
A feast is not a snack. We sit down, we take our time, and we enjoy it. That is how the scriptures can become a part of us.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time their faith grew or was tested. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Peter and the storm

blocks.text: The disciples were crossing the lake at night, and the wind was against them. Jesus Christ came to them, walking on the water. Peter called out, asking to come to Him.

And Peter answered him and said, Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water.
And he said, Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus.
But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.
And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?

Peter did what no one else in the boat did. He stepped out. When he looked at the Savior, he walked. When he looked at the wind, he sank. Notice that even then, he did not drown. He cried out, and the Savior’s hand was already there.

application.text: What can we do this week? Let me offer three small steps.
First, begin each day with a short prayer. Thank God for one thing, and ask for help with one thing.
Second, read the scriptures daily, even for five minutes. Look for one verse that speaks to your situation.
Third, act on one prompting you have been putting off. It might be a call to make, an apology to give, or a service to offer.
If you feel your faith is small, remember Alma. A desire to believe is enough to begin.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God lives, and that Jesus Christ is His Son and my Savior. I know that He keeps His promises. I know that faith grows as we act on it, and that He is near to those who trust Him. I say this in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Think about how your day began. You probably reached for something without thinking. A light switch. A phone. A cup of water. You did not stop to ask if the light would come on. You trusted that it would.
We live on trust more than we notice. We trust the bus to come. We trust a friend to keep a promise. We plant a seed and trust that something will grow.
Faith in Jesus Christ is trust of a deeper kind. It reaches past what we can see. It rests on the Savior, on who He is, and on what He has promised.
Today I want to speak about what faith is, where it comes from, what it does for us, and how we can make it stronger. I pray that each of us will leave a little more sure of Him.

mainMessage.text: Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ is the first principle of the gospel. It is a gift from God. It comes as we hear His word, and it grows as we act on it.

blocks.text: If someone asks what the first principle of the gospel is, many of us say, faith. That is right. But the fuller answer is faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Faith needs something to rest on. Ours rests on the Savior.
Paul wrote to the Hebrew Saints at a time when their faith was being tested. He told them what faith is.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

Two phrases stand out here: things hoped for, and evidence. Faith is not a wish. It is a hope that stands on something real. The Joseph Smith Translation uses the word assurance. Faith gives us a quiet assurance about what God has promised, even before we see it.

Alma taught the same truth to a poor group of Zoramites who had been driven out of their places of worship. They were humble, and they wanted to know how to begin. Alma told them that faith is not perfect knowledge.
And now as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true.
That is good news for us. We do not have to know everything before we start. We start with what we hope is true, and we act on it.
Faith is also more than believing that Jesus Christ lived. Many people believe He lived. Faith means trusting that He is the Son of God, that He atoned for our sins, and that He keeps His promises.
President Russell M. Nelson taught how much this trust can do for us. In his talk “Christ Is Risen; Faith in Him Will Move Mountains,” he said:
Jesus Christ will increase your ability to move the mountains in your life.

What are the mountains in your life? A sickness. A broken relationship. A fear about the future. Faith does not always remove the mountain. But it gives us strength to climb it, and sometimes the Savior moves it for us.
President James E. Faust spoke about the hope that goes with faith. In his talk “Hope, an Anchor of the Soul,” from the October 1999 general conference, he said:
Hope is trust in God’s promises, faith that if we act now, the desired blessings will be fulfilled in the future.
Where does faith come from? Paul answered this when he wrote to the Saints in Rome.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

Faith comes by hearing. That means we have some choice in how strong it becomes. We can choose what we hear. We can fill our days with voices that pull us away, or we can make room for the word of God.

The best way is to read the scriptures every day. Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained why, in his talk “Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation,” from the October 2006 general conference. He said:

When we want to speak to God, we pray. And when we want Him to speak to us, we search the scriptures; for His words are spoken through His prophets. He will then teach us as we listen to the promptings of the Holy Spirit.
Prayer is how we speak to God. The scriptures are one of the ways He speaks to us. A little time each day keeps that conversation going, and it builds faith.
Mormon saw this in the history of the Nephites. He wrote about what happens to those who lay hold upon the word of God.

Yea, we see that whosoever will may lay hold upon the word of God, which is quick and powerful, which shall divide asunder all the cunning and the snares and the wiles of the devil, and lead the man of Christ in a strait and narrow course across that everlasting gulf of misery which is prepared to engulf the wicked—
Another place we hear the word of God is general conference, when the prophets and apostles speak to us.
If we listen with a question in our hearts, we will often find the answer in the very next talk. Faith grows in those moments.
Faith is not only something we feel. It is something we do. James wrote to the scattered Saints because some of them said they believed but did not live like it.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
Think of a boat with one oar. It goes in circles. Faith and works are the two oars. We need both to move forward. Belief without action stays in place. Action without belief has no direction.

This is not a new problem. When John the Baptist taught the people, some of them said, “We are children of Abraham.” They thought their family line was enough. John told them to bring forth fruits that showed they had really repented. Saying we believe is not the same as living what we believe.

Then said he to the multitude that came forth to be baptized of him, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, That God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.

Faith shows up in small things. It is the person who forgives when it would be easier to stay angry. It is the family that prays together even when everyone is tired. It is the young man who stays true when his friends laugh. It is what we do on a Tuesday afternoon, not only what we say on Sunday.
And faith is a gift from God. We do not make it from nothing. We ask for it in prayer, and we make room for it by how we live. When we act on the little faith we have, God adds to it.

When we act on our faith, God can work in our lives. Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained how faith grows stronger, in his talk “The Sustaining Power of Faith in Times of Uncertainty and Testing,” from the April 2003 general conference. He said:

You can learn to use faith more effectively by applying this principle taught by Moroni: ‘. . . ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith’ \[Ether 12:6; italics added\]. Thus, every time you try your faith, that is, act in worthiness on an impression, you will receive the confirming evidence of the Spirit. Those feelings will fortify your faith. As you repeat that pattern, your faith will become stronger.
Many people say they would believe if they could see a sign. But the Lord teaches that the order is the other way. He spoke to the early Saints through the Prophet Joseph Smith about this.

But, behold, faith cometh not by signs, but signs follow those that believe.
Yea, signs come by faith, not by the will of men, nor as they please, but by the will of God.
Signs follow faith. They do not come before it. Moroni taught the same thing when he wrote about the faith of the people in his record.

And now, I, Moroni, would speak somewhat concerning these things; I would show unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.
The witness comes after the trial of our faith. That is hard to hear, because trials are never fun. But it means that the days we feel least sure may be the days our faith is being built.
Seeing a miracle does not make faith strong by itself. Laman and Lemuel saw an angel. They still murmured and doubted.
And it came to pass as they smote us with a rod, behold, an angel of the Lord came and stood before them, and he spake unto them, saying: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod?
Faith is not about seeing. It is about choosing to trust God, again and again, before we see.
We may not need a miracle today. But we all need strength for hard days. We need it for illness, for work, for loneliness, and for waiting.

Faith does not always bring the answer we ask for. Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about this in his talk “Healing the Sick,” from the April 2010 general conference. He said:

As we exercise the undoubted power of the priesthood of God and as we treasure His promise that He will hear and answer the prayer of faith, we must always remember that faith and the healing power of the priesthood cannot produce a result contrary to the will of Him whose priesthood it is.
God hears the prayer of faith, and His will is wiser than ours. Even when the answer is not what we hoped for, His strength is real, and we do not carry the load alone.
The Savior makes this promise to all who trust Him. Paul reminded the Hebrew Saints of it when they were facing hardship.

Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.

God will not leave us. Paul also showed the Saints a long line of people who trusted God before them, such as Abraham, Moses, and many others. They did not all see the end of their trials in this life. But they held on, and God kept His promises to them.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Helaman wrote to Captain Moroni about his own people in a time of great danger and weakness. They poured out their souls to God, and He gave them assurance and peace.

Therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.
Yea, and it came to pass that the Lord our God did visit us with assurances that he would deliver us; yea, insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him.
Faith does not remove our trials. It gives us strength to go through them, because the Savior walks with us.

If faith is a gift that grows, how do we feed it? Alma gave the Zoramites a picture they could understand. He compared faith to a seed. He told them to begin with a desire to believe, and to let that desire work in them.

But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.
Now, we will compare the word unto a seed. Now, if ye give place, that a seed may be planted in your heart, behold, if it be a true seed, or a good seed, if ye do not cast it out by your unbelief, that ye will resist the Spirit of the Lord, behold, it will begin to swell within your breasts; and when you feel these swelling motions, ye will begin to say within yourselves—It must needs be that this is a good seed, or that the word is good, for it beginneth to enlarge my soul; yea, it beginneth to enlighten my understanding, yea, it beginneth to be delicious to me.
A seed does not grow in one day. We plant it, water it, and give it light. We do not dig it up every morning to see if it is growing. We trust, and we keep caring for it.
Alma also warned what happens when we neglect it. A tree with no care does not grow roots. When the heat of the sun comes, it dries up. But a tree that is fed grows into something strong.

But if ye neglect the tree, and take no thought for its nourishment, behold it will not get any root; and when the heat of the sun cometh and scorcheth it, because it hath no root it withers away, and ye pluck it up and cast it out.
But if ye will nourish the word, yea, nourish the tree as it beginneth to grow, by your faith with great diligence, and with patience, looking forward to the fruit thereof, it shall take root; and behold it shall be a tree springing up unto everlasting life.

How do we feed it? Nephi taught that we press forward with a steadfast faith in Christ and feast on His word. We pray each day. We read the scriptures. We fast. We keep our covenants. We serve others.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught what it means to feast. In his talk “Living by Scriptural Guidance,” from the October 2000 general conference, he said:

To feast means to savor. We savor the scriptures by studying them in a spirit of delightful discovery and faithful obedience. When we feast upon the words of Christ, they . . . become an integral part of our nature.
None of these is big. But together, done every day, they grow a faith that will not wither in the heat.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time their faith grew or was tested. If they have no story of their own, the app offers these from the scriptures. The member taps one to add it, and can still change the words.
story.title: Peter walks on the water

blocks.text:
And Peter answered him and said, Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water.
And he said, Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus.
But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.
And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?

The disciples were in a boat in the night, and the wind was against them. The Savior came to them walking on the sea. Peter asked to come to Him, and the Savior said, Come. Peter stepped out and walked. Then he looked at the strong wind and became afraid, and he began to sink. He cried out, Lord, save me. At once the Savior reached out His hand and caught him. When Peter kept his eyes on the Savior, he did what he could not do alone. When he looked at the storm, he sank. We can do the same. Faith keeps our eyes on Him.

Thou shalt construct a ship, after the manner which I shall show thee, that I may carry thy people across these waters.
And I said: Lord, whither shall I go that I may find ore to molten, that I may make tools to construct the ship after the manner which thou hast shown unto me?
And it came to pass that the Lord told me whither I should go to find ore, that I might make tools.

The Lord told Nephi to build a ship, and Nephi had never built one. His brothers laughed at him and said he was foolish. Nephi did not argue about whether it could be done. He asked the Lord where to find ore to make tools. The Lord showed him, and he got to work. Later, when his brothers wanted to harm him, the Lord filled Nephi with power, and they could not touch him. Nephi did not wait to understand everything. He took the next step the Lord gave him. That is faith in action.

alternatives.title: The brother of Jared and the stones

blocks.text: And I know, O Lord, that thou hast all power, and can do whatsoever thou wilt for the benefit of man; therefore touch these stones, O Lord, with thy finger, and prepare them that they may shine forth in darkness; and they shall shine forth unto us in the vessels which we have prepared, that we may have light while we shall cross the sea.

The brother of Jared and his people had to cross the sea in small, tight boats with no light inside. The Lord told him to find a way to bring light. He did not just ask for it. He worked first. He made sixteen small stones, and then he prayed and asked the Lord to touch them. Because he had done his part and trusted the Lord to do His, the Lord touched the stones, and the boats had light. Faith led him to work, and then to ask.

application.text: So what can we do this week? Let me suggest three small acts of faith.
First, pray each morning. Start by saying thank you before you ask for anything. Then ask God for one thing you need help with that day.
Second, read a few verses of scripture every day. It does not have to be long. Read, think about it, and write down one thing you learned.
Third, keep one promise you made to God. It may be your baptismal covenant, a commitment to pay tithing, or a calling you have been putting off. Choose one, and keep it, even when it is not easy.

If you feel your faith is small, do not worry. Alma taught that a desire to believe is enough to begin. Start there, and care for it every day. Think of one mountain in your life. Then ask what one step of faith you could take toward it this week.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words here. The app offers these lines to those who need help:

blocks.text: I know that God lives and that Jesus Christ is my Savior. I know that He atoned for my sins and that He keeps His promises. I know that faith grows as we act on it, and that He helps us when we trust Him. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Picture someone walking a country road at night with a lantern. The light does not reach the end of the road. It reaches only a few steps ahead. But every time the traveler takes those steps, the light moves forward and shows a few more.
That is a good picture of faith. God rarely lights the whole road for us. He lights the next few steps and asks us to walk.
Today I would like to speak about faith in Jesus Christ. I will share what it is, where it comes from, what it can do for us, and how we can care for it.

mainMessage.text: Faith in Jesus Christ is a gift from God. We receive it as we hear His word, and we keep it as we choose to trust Him and act.

blocks.text: If you asked a hundred members of the Church for the first principle of the gospel, most would say, faith. The full answer has a name in it: faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Faith is never only an idea. It is trust in a person.
Paul wrote to Hebrew Saints who were under pressure, and he gave them a clear description.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Substance and evidence are strong words. They tell us faith has weight. It is not weak or vague. It stands on what God has shown us.
Alma spoke to the Zoramites, who had been driven from their places of worship and were humble because of it. He wanted them to know that they did not need to wait for perfect knowledge.
And now as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true.
So we start where we are. We hold on to what is true, and we hope for the rest.
President Russell M. Nelson spoke about what Jesus Christ can do when we trust Him. In his talk “Christ Is Risen; Faith in Him Will Move Mountains,” from the April 2021 general conference, he said:
Jesus Christ will increase your ability to move the mountains in your life.

Notice the words “increase your ability.” He does not always take the mountain away. He gives us the strength to climb it. Think about the mountain you are facing, and ask whether you have invited Him to help.
President James E. Faust taught how hope fits with faith. In his talk “Hope, an Anchor of the Soul,” from the October 1999 general conference, he said:
Hope is trust in God’s promises, faith that if we act now, the desired blessings will be fulfilled in the future.
Hope looks forward. Faith acts now. Together they hold us steady.
Where does faith come from? Paul answered plainly when he wrote to the Saints in Rome.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
If faith comes by hearing the word of God, then the way to grow it is to listen to that word. We cannot make faith by forcing it. But we can place ourselves where it grows.
Mormon paused in his record of the Nephites to teach what the word of God can do.

Yea, we see that whosoever will may lay hold upon the word of God, which is quick and powerful, which shall divide asunder all the cunning and the snares and the wiles of the devil, and lead the man of Christ in a strait and narrow course across that everlasting gulf of misery which is prepared to engulf the wicked—
To lay hold means to grip firmly. Think of a rope across a river. We do not touch it now and then. We hold on.

Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught how prayer and scripture work together. In his talk “Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

When we want to speak to God, we pray. And when we want Him to speak to us, we search the scriptures; for His words are spoken through His prophets. He will then teach us as we listen to the promptings of the Holy Spirit.

If we want God to speak to us, we know where to go. We open the scriptures, and we listen for the Holy Ghost. We can also listen when the prophets and apostles speak at general conference. Faith is being fed each time.
Faith does not stay in the mind. It goes into our hands and feet. James wrote to Saints who talked about believing but did not live as if they did.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
A person can say he has a map, but if he never walks the road, the map has done him no good. In the same way, belief that never leads to action is not yet living faith.
When John the Baptist preached repentance, some in the crowd thought it did not apply to them. They were descendants of Abraham, they said, and so they were safe.

Then said he to the multitude that came forth to be baptized of him, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, That God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
John did not accept family heritage as a substitute for change. He asked for fruits.

What are fruits today? Showing up to serve in a calling when we are tired. Telling the truth when it is costly. Praying with our children when the day has been long. Faith shows itself in what we do when no one is watching.

Faith is not only a comfort. It is a power. When we act on it, God is able to work in our lives. Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described how this power builds. In his talk “The Sustaining Power of Faith in Times of Uncertainty and Testing,” from the April 2003 general conference, he said:

You can learn to use faith more effectively by applying this principle taught by Moroni: ‘. . . ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith’ \[Ether 12:6; italics added\]. Thus, every time you try your faith, that is, act in worthiness on an impression, you will receive the confirming evidence of the Spirit. Those feelings will fortify your faith. As you repeat that pattern, your faith will become stronger.
There is a cycle in that. We receive an impression, we act in worthiness, the Spirit confirms, and our faith grows. Each time we go around the cycle, we are stronger.
Moroni explained the same truth in his own words, as he taught about faith near the end of his record.

And now, I, Moroni, would speak somewhat concerning these things; I would show unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.
The Lord also taught this in our day. Some Saints wanted signs first, and the Lord corrected the order through the Prophet Joseph Smith.

But, behold, faith cometh not by signs, but signs follow those that believe.
Yea, signs come by faith, not by the will of men, nor as they please, but by the will of God.
A sign does not create faith. Faith comes first, and the evidence follows. Even a great sign can be forgotten. When Laman and Lemuel were beating their younger brothers, an angel appeared to them.
And it came to pass as they smote us with a rod, behold, an angel of the Lord came and stood before them, and he spake unto them, saying: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod?
They saw an angel, and shortly after they were murmuring. What they lacked was not evidence. It was a willing heart.
None of us walk a smooth road all the way. There are seasons of loss, illness, worry, and waiting. Faith is most needed then.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave honest counsel. In his talk “Healing the Sick,” from the April 2010 general conference, he said:

As we exercise the undoubted power of the priesthood of God and as we treasure His promise that He will hear and answer the prayer of faith, we must always remember that faith and the healing power of the priesthood cannot produce a result contrary to the will of Him whose priesthood it is.
This tells us that faith is trust in God’s will, not a way to bend God to ours. When the answer is not what we asked for, we can trust that God sees more than we do.
Paul wrote to Saints who were facing hardship, and he told them what the Lord had promised.

Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.
When we feel alone, we can hold on to those words. God has said it, and He does not break His word.
Paul also reminded them of faithful people from earlier ages who endured much.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
They kept going without seeing the end. They trusted that God would do what He said.
Helaman wrote to Captain Moroni about a time when his people felt weak, and it seemed that they might lose everything.

Therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.
Yea, and it came to pass that the Lord our God did visit us with assurances that he would deliver us; yea, insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him.
They did not have a plan to win. They had a prayer. God answered with peace and with more faith than they had before.
Faith needs tending. If we are not careful, it can fade. Alma used a seed to show how it grows.

But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.
Now, we will compare the word unto a seed. Now, if ye give place, that a seed may be planted in your heart, behold, if it be a true seed, or a good seed, if ye do not cast it out by your unbelief, that ye will resist the Spirit of the Lord, behold, it will begin to swell within your breasts; and when you feel these swelling motions, ye will begin to say within yourselves—It must needs be that this is a good seed, or that the word is good, for it beginneth to enlarge my soul; yea, it beginneth to enlighten my understanding, yea, it beginneth to be delicious to me.
Alma asked for an experiment. Give the word a place. Notice what happens inside. If it enlarges your soul and enlightens your understanding, you have found something good.
Then comes the care. Alma told them that the tree needs nourishment.

But if ye neglect the tree, and take no thought for its nourishment, behold it will not get any root; and when the heat of the sun cometh and scorcheth it, because it hath no root it withers away, and ye pluck it up and cast it out.
But if ye will nourish the word, yea, nourish the tree as it beginneth to grow, by your faith with great diligence, and with patience, looking forward to the fruit thereof, it shall take root; and behold it shall be a tree springing up unto everlasting life.
Diligence and patience. Those two words are what a gardener needs, and they are what a person of faith needs. Nephi gave a pattern for what to do.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described what feasting means. In his talk “Living by Scriptural Guidance,” from the October 2000 general conference, he said:

To feast means to savor. We savor the scriptures by studying them in a spirit of delightful discovery and faithful obedience. When we feast upon the words of Christ, they . . . become an integral part of our nature.
The words of Christ become part of our nature. That is the goal. Faith is no longer something we turn on in an emergency. It is who we are.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time their faith grew or was tested. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Nephi and the ship

blocks.text: The Lord told Nephi to build a ship. Nephi had never built a ship in his life.

Thou shalt construct a ship, after the manner which I shall show thee, that I may carry thy people across these waters.
And I said: Lord, whither shall I go that I may find ore to molten, that I may make tools to construct the ship after the manner which thou hast shown unto me?
And it came to pass that the Lord told me whither I should go to find ore, that I might make tools.

His brothers laughed at him and said he was a fool. Nephi did not argue that he was able. He asked where to find ore, and the Lord showed him. Then he began to work. Nephi had faith that the Lord would guide each step, and the Lord did.

application.text: Let me offer three ways to act this week.
First, pick one hard thing in front of you and pray about it by name. Ask God what the next step is, and then listen.
Second, set aside a regular time each day for the scriptures. Choose a time you can keep, even if it is short.
Third, do one thing you feel the Spirit has asked of you. Do it before you feel fully ready.
If your faith feels small, take courage from Alma. A desire to believe, kept alive, can grow into something strong.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God lives and loves us. I know that Jesus Christ is my Savior and Redeemer. I know that when we trust Him, He leads us one step at a time. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Think about the last time you saw a house being built. Before the walls go up, workers dig, pour, and level. For weeks it looks like nothing is happening. But everything that comes later rests on that work. If the foundation is weak, the house will not stand.

Our lives are the same. We build every day. We build families, friendships, work, and habits. The question is what we are building on. Today I want to talk about the one foundation that does not move. It is faith in Jesus Christ.

mainMessage.text: Faith in Jesus Christ is the first principle of the gospel, and it is where we start. It is not a feeling that comes and goes. It is trust in Him that leads us to act. When we build on that trust, we can stand through storms. And when our faith needs repair, we can rebuild it, one stone at a time.

blocks.text: What is the foundation made of? Paul gave a short and famous answer.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Substance and evidence are solid words. They are not wishes. Paul is telling us that faith has weight. It is real, even when we cannot see everything it points to.
Alma added something that gives many of us comfort. He said that faith is not the same as knowing everything.
And now as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true.
Notice the last words: “which are true.” We do not hope in something made up. We hope in what is true, even before we can see all of it.
President Russell M. Nelson has taught what this kind of faith can do. In his talk “Overcome the World and Find Rest,” from the April 2021 general conference, he said:
Jesus Christ will increase your ability to move the mountains in your life.
He did not say that the mountains disappear. He said our ability to move them grows. That is how a strong foundation works. It does not remove the weight. It carries it.
Elder James E. Faust of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles tied faith and hope together. In his talk “The Anchor of Hope,” from the October 1999 general conference, he said:
Hope is trust in God’s promises, faith that if we act now, the desired blessings will be fulfilled in the future.
See the two words in the middle: “act now.” A foundation is something we do, not something we only admire.
A builder needs material. Where do we get the stones for our faith? Paul told us plainly.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Faith grows when we take in the word of God. We hear it, read it, and think about it. Without it, the foundation stays thin.
Helaman taught the same idea with a powerful picture. He said the word of God is a guide through dangerous ground.

Yea, we see that whosoever will may lay hold upon the word of God, which is quick and powerful, which shall divide asunder all the cunning and the snares and the wiles of the devil, and lead the man of Christ in a strait and narrow course across that everlasting gulf of misery which is prepared to engulf the wicked—
The words “whosoever will” are an open door. No one is left out. Anyone who chooses to lay hold of the word can be led safely across.

Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained how this works in practice. In his talk “Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto the Salvation of Men,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

When we want to speak to God, we pray. And when we want Him to speak to us, we search the scriptures; for His words are spoken through His prophets. He will then teach us as we listen to the promptings of the Holy Spirit.
So prayer and scripture work together. In prayer we speak. In the scriptures He speaks. A home that has both has good building material.
A foundation that never has a house on it is a waste. Faith is meant to hold something up. James said it directly.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
Faith that stays in the mind is not enough. It has to show up in what we do. That might be a kind word, a visit, a prayer, or a choice to keep a commitment.
John the Baptist said something similar to a crowd that was proud of its heritage.

Then said he to the multitude that came forth to be baptized of him, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, That God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
The people leaned on their family name. John told them that a name is not a foundation. Fruits are. The way we live shows what we are standing on.

A good foundation holds a lot of weight. Faith does the same. It carries us when we cannot carry ourselves. And the more we use it, the stronger it gets. Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this clearly. In his talk “The Sustaining Power of Faith in Times of Uncertainty and Testing,” from the April 2003 general conference, he said:

You can learn to use faith more effectively by applying this principle taught by Moroni: ‘. . . ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith’ \[Ether 12:6; italics added\]. Thus, every time you try your faith, that is, act in worthiness on an impression, you will receive the confirming evidence of the Spirit. Those feelings will fortify your faith. As you repeat that pattern, your faith will become stronger.
Picture a builder adding one course of stone at a time. Each time we act on an impression, we add a stone. The Spirit confirms it. Then we add another. Over time, we have a wall.
Here is the principle Elder Scott was quoting. Moroni wrote it for people who wanted proof before they would believe.

And now, I, Moroni, would speak somewhat concerning these things; I would show unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.
The witness comes after the trial. We build first. Then we see what the building can hold.
The Lord gave Joseph Smith the same order in our day.

But, behold, faith cometh not by signs, but signs follow those that believe.
Yea, signs come by faith, not by the will of men, nor as they please, but by the will of God.
No one builds a house by asking for the finished rooms first. We start with the foundation, and the rest follows in its season.
Even a miracle does not replace a willing heart. Think of Laman and Lemuel, who saw an angel with their own eyes.
And it came to pass as they smote us with a rod, behold, an angel of the Lord came and stood before them, and he spake unto them, saying: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod?
An angel stood in front of them. And yet it did not last. Their trouble was not a lack of signs. It was a hard heart.
Sooner or later, every house faces weather. Illness comes. A job is lost. A loved one passes. A prayer seems to go unanswered. This is when we find out what we built on.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke with honesty about this. In his talk “Healing the Sick,” from the April 2010 general conference, he said:

As we exercise the undoubted power of the priesthood of God and as we treasure His promise that He will hear and answer the prayer of faith, we must always remember that faith and the healing power of the priesthood cannot produce a result contrary to the will of Him whose priesthood it is.
That is not an easy truth. But it is a steadying one. Faith is not a lever that makes God do what we want. It is trust that He knows more than we do, and that He cares.
Paul wrote to Saints who knew trouble well. He reminded them of a promise.

Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.
“I will never leave thee.” In the worst week of your life, that sentence is still true.
Paul also pointed to people who lived and died holding on to what God had promised them.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
They did not see every promise come true in their lifetime. They still kept faith. That is a kind of strength that only a deep foundation can give.
Helaman wrote to Captain Moroni from a hard place. His small army was worn down, and help was slow to arrive.

Therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.
Yea, and it came to pass that the Lord our God did visit us with assurances that he would deliver us; yea, insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him.
They prayed. And God gave them peace, along with more faith. Sometimes that is the first answer we get. It is not a way out, but strength to stay standing.
Even a strong house needs care. Roofs leak. Paint peels. Faith is no different. Alma taught us how to look after it, using the picture of a seed that becomes a tree.

But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.
Now, we will compare the word unto a seed. Now, if ye give place, that a seed may be planted in your heart, behold, if it be a true seed, or a good seed, if ye do not cast it out by your unbelief, that ye will resist the Spirit of the Lord, behold, it will begin to swell within your breasts; and when you feel these swelling motions, ye will begin to say within yourselves—It must needs be that this is a good seed, or that the word is good, for it beginneth to enlarge my soul; yea, it beginneth to enlighten my understanding, yea, it beginneth to be delicious to me.
You can start with a small desire. Alma says that is enough to begin. Then you watch what happens in you.
After the planting comes the daily work.

But if ye neglect the tree, and take no thought for its nourishment, behold it will not get any root; and when the heat of the sun cometh and scorcheth it, because it hath no root it withers away, and ye pluck it up and cast it out.
But if ye will nourish the word, yea, nourish the tree as it beginneth to grow, by your faith with great diligence, and with patience, looking forward to the fruit thereof, it shall take root; and behold it shall be a tree springing up unto everlasting life.
Roots are what keep a tree standing when the wind blows. They grow out of sight, in ordinary days. The daily habits we keep are our roots.
Nephi gave us a simple path to follow.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained what it means to feast. In his talk “Living by Scriptural Guidance,” from the October 2000 general conference, he said:

To feast means to savor. We savor the scriptures by studying them in a spirit of delightful discovery and faithful obedience. When we feast upon the words of Christ, they . . . become an integral part of our nature.
A meal is not rushed. We sit, taste, and enjoy it. When we read the scriptures that way, they become part of who we are, and our foundation gets deeper.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time their faith was tested or built up. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The brother of Jared and the stones

blocks.text: The brother of Jared and his people had built eight small barges. But there was a problem. The barges had no light inside. He took the problem to the Lord. Then he did something. He went up a mountain with sixteen small stones he had made himself, and he prayed.

And I know, O Lord, that thou hast all power, and can do whatsoever thou wilt for the benefit of man; therefore touch these stones, O Lord, with thy finger, and prepare them that they may shine forth in darkness; and they shall shine forth unto us in the vessels which we have prepared, that we may have light while we shall cross the sea.
He did the work he could do. He made the stones. Then he asked the Lord to do what only the Lord could do. That is faith in action. We prepare what is in our hands, and we trust God with the rest.

application.text: Here are three ways to strengthen your foundation this week.
First, name one place where you are waiting on the Lord. Write it down. Then write one small thing you can do about it today, and do it.
Second, add one stone. Pick a single scripture, read it slowly, and think about it. Do this each day for seven days.
Third, let someone see your faith. Share a short thought with a family member or friend. Faith grows when we say it out loud.
If you feel your foundation is shaky, do not give up on the house. Start with a desire to believe. Alma said that is enough to begin.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the sure foundation. I know He lives. I know that when we build on Him, the storms may come, but we will not fall. I leave this testimony with you in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: A sailor far out at sea has no road signs. There is water in every direction. So what does the sailor do? He trusts the compass. He cannot see the harbor. But the needle points the same way every time, and he steers by it.
Life can feel like open water. We do not always see where a choice will lead. Faith in Jesus Christ is how we steer when we cannot see the shore. Let me share what the scriptures say about it.

mainMessage.text: Faith in Jesus Christ is trusting Him enough to follow Him. It begins with a desire, grows as we take in His word, and shows itself in what we do. It does not remove every storm. But it keeps us pointed the right way, even when the shore is out of sight.

blocks.text: What is faith, exactly? Paul gave us a short definition that people have quoted for two thousand years.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

The sailor has not seen the harbor, yet he has good reason to believe it is there. That is the meaning of “evidence of things not seen.” Faith rests on real reasons, even when the whole picture is still ahead of us.
Alma helped us understand what faith does not require.
And now as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true.
You do not need a perfect map to begin. You need a true direction. And we have one, because the things we hope for “are true.”
President Russell M. Nelson has promised us help along the way. In his talk “Overcome the World and Find Rest,” from the April 2021 general conference, he said:
Jesus Christ will increase your ability to move the mountains in your life.
That promise is personal. It says “your ability” and “your life.” The Savior is not far off. He works with each of us on the mountains we face.
Elder James E. Faust of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described how faith and hope work as a pair. In his talk “The Anchor of Hope,” from the October 1999 general conference, he said:
Hope is trust in God’s promises, faith that if we act now, the desired blessings will be fulfilled in the future.
A compass is useless if you leave it in the drawer. It only helps when you look at it and act on what it says. Hope is the same. It points toward blessings, and faith moves us toward them now.
A compass has to be read. How do we learn to read the direction God is pointing us? Paul answered in one sentence.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
The more we hear His word, the more clearly we can tell where it points. We learn it the way a sailor learns the sea, through steady practice.
Helaman taught that God’s word is a guide for crossing dangerous waters.

Yea, we see that whosoever will may lay hold upon the word of God, which is quick and powerful, which shall divide asunder all the cunning and the snares and the wiles of the devil, and lead the man of Christ in a strait and narrow course across that everlasting gulf of misery which is prepared to engulf the wicked—

Look at the phrase “a strait and narrow course.” That is the language of navigation. The word of God keeps us on the course and away from the rocks. And it is for “whosoever will.” Anyone may take hold of it.

Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught how to use both prayer and scripture. In his talk “Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto the Salvation of Men,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

When we want to speak to God, we pray. And when we want Him to speak to us, we search the scriptures; for His words are spoken through His prophets. He will then teach us as we listen to the promptings of the Holy Spirit.
So when we want direction, we do two things. We ask in prayer, and we search the scriptures. Then we listen for the Spirit to teach us.
Owning a compass will not get you home. You have to sail. James said faith works the same way.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
Saying we believe is easy. Living it takes effort. When James asks to be shown faith by works, he is asking whether our choices follow our beliefs.
John the Baptist faced a crowd that thought belonging to the right family was enough.

Then said he to the multitude that came forth to be baptized of him, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, That God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
They were pointing at their ancestors. John pointed them back to their own lives. Our heritage is a gift, but it does not do our sailing for us. Each of us has to set the course and move.

A ship has sails and an engine. Faith has power too. It moves us forward when we would otherwise stand still. Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained how that power grows. In his talk “The Sustaining Power of Faith in Times of Uncertainty and Testing,” from the April 2003 general conference, he said:

You can learn to use faith more effectively by applying this principle taught by Moroni: ‘. . . ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith’ \[Ether 12:6; italics added\]. Thus, every time you try your faith, that is, act in worthiness on an impression, you will receive the confirming evidence of the Spirit. Those feelings will fortify your faith. As you repeat that pattern, your faith will become stronger.
Think of a sailor who learns the wind by sailing. Each trip teaches him something. We learn faith the same way. We act on an impression, we see the Spirit confirm it, and next time we trust it more.
Moroni wrote the principle for people who wanted proof first.

And now, I, Moroni, would speak somewhat concerning these things; I would show unto the world that faith is things which are hoped for and not seen; wherefore, dispute not because ye see not, for ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith.
The order matters. Trial first, then witness. We cast off before the harbor shows itself.
The Lord restored the same truth in our day.

But, behold, faith cometh not by signs, but signs follow those that believe.
Yea, signs come by faith, not by the will of men, nor as they please, but by the will of God.
We do not get to set the terms. The Lord gives evidence in His own time and His own way. Our part is to believe and to move.
Even seeing a miracle does not guarantee faith. Nephi and Sam were struck by their older brothers, and an angel came.
And it came to pass as they smote us with a rod, behold, an angel of the Lord came and stood before them, and he spake unto them, saying: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod?
Seeing an angel did not turn Laman and Lemuel around for long. What changes a heart is not only what we see. It is what we choose.

Every voyage meets weather. We may face sickness, money trouble, a broken relationship, or a long season of waiting. The sailor does not throw the compass overboard when the waves rise. He holds it tighter.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave wise counsel about faith in hard times. In his talk “Healing the Sick,” from the April 2010 general conference, he said:

As we exercise the undoubted power of the priesthood of God and as we treasure His promise that He will hear and answer the prayer of faith, we must always remember that faith and the healing power of the priesthood cannot produce a result contrary to the will of Him whose priesthood it is.
This means faith includes trusting His will. We ask with all our heart. And we leave the result with the One who sees the whole sea.
Paul wrote to people in difficult days. He gave them words to hold on to.

Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.
He said, “I will never leave thee.” No wave is too big for that promise. You are not sailing alone.
Paul also looked back at faithful men and women who did not live to see everything fulfilled.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
They saw the promises from far away. They did not turn back. Sometimes faith means steering toward a shore we will only reach later.
Helaman wrote to Captain Moroni about his own storm. His men were few, and the pressure was heavy.

Therefore we did pour out our souls in prayer to God, that he would strengthen us and deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.
Yea, and it came to pass that the Lord our God did visit us with assurances that he would deliver us; yea, insomuch that he did speak peace to our souls, and did grant unto us great faith, and did cause us that we should hope for our deliverance in him.
Their answer was peace and stronger faith. The waves did not stop at once. But they were steady inside, and that made all the difference.
A good sailor checks his heading often. A small error today can put him far from the harbor next week. Faith needs the same care. Alma showed us how with the picture of a seed.

But behold, if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words, and exercise a particle of faith, yea, even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you, even until ye believe in a manner that ye can give place for a portion of my words.
Now, we will compare the word unto a seed. Now, if ye give place, that a seed may be planted in your heart, behold, if it be a true seed, or a good seed, if ye do not cast it out by your unbelief, that ye will resist the Spirit of the Lord, behold, it will begin to swell within your breasts; and when you feel these swelling motions, ye will begin to say within yourselves—It must needs be that this is a good seed, or that the word is good, for it beginneth to enlarge my soul; yea, it beginneth to enlighten my understanding, yea, it beginneth to be delicious to me.
Try the word. See what it does in you. If it enlarges your soul and brings light to your mind, you have found a true direction.
Then keep going. A good start is not a finished trip.

But if ye neglect the tree, and take no thought for its nourishment, behold it will not get any root; and when the heat of the sun cometh and scorcheth it, because it hath no root it withers away, and ye pluck it up and cast it out.
But if ye will nourish the word, yea, nourish the tree as it beginneth to grow, by your faith with great diligence, and with patience, looking forward to the fruit thereof, it shall take root; and behold it shall be a tree springing up unto everlasting life.
Neglect is what harms faith most. Small daily care is what keeps it alive. A few minutes with the word each day keeps the heading true.
Nephi gave a clear instruction for the whole journey.

Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained the word “feasting.” In his talk “Living by Scriptural Guidance,” from the October 2000 general conference, he said:

To feast means to savor. We savor the scriptures by studying them in a spirit of delightful discovery and faithful obedience. When we feast upon the words of Christ, they . . . become an integral part of our nature.
A compass in your pocket is good. A direction in your nature is better. That is what feasting on His words can do for us.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time their faith guided a choice, or was tested. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The woman who touched the Savior’s garment

blocks.text: For twelve years a woman had suffered from a constant illness. She had no cure and no hope from others. Then she heard about Jesus. She chose to go to Him.

When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment.
For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole.
And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up; and she felt in her body that she was healed of that plague.
The crowd was thick. She was weak. Still, she turned toward Him and reached out. Then the Savior spoke to her.
And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.
She set her course on Jesus and moved. That is faith. She did not wait until it was easy. She reached out in the middle of the crowd, and He answered her.

application.text: Here are three ways to set your course this week.
First, think of a decision you are facing. Ask yourself, “What would Jesus Christ want me to do here?” Pray about it, and then act on what you feel.
Second, check your heading every day. Spend a few quiet minutes in the scriptures, even if it is only a few verses.
Third, reach out to someone who is struggling. Faith grows when we help others find their way.
If you feel far from shore, remember that you do not need a perfect map. You need to keep turning toward Him.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. I know that He lives and that He guides those who follow Him. I know that when we turn toward Him, even in the dark, He leads us home. I say this in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
